title: Seven verses, said seventeen times a day
hookLine: the Fatiha is recited in every unit of every prayer

cards: Do some arithmetic with a Muslim who prays all five daily prayers. Dawn has two units of prayer, called rak'ahs. Noon has four.
Afternoon, four. Sunset, three. Night, four.
That's seventeen. And in every one of those seventeen units, standing, the same short surah is recited. Seventeen times a day, before any optional prayers are counted.
Over a year, more than six thousand times, from the same seven verses. Today: seven verses.

teach.b: Last year you learned al-Fatiha a line at a time. This year, step back and look at the whole surah, and at what repetition does to words.

The rule comes from a hadith in Bukhari and Muslim: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said there is no prayer for the one who does not recite the Opening of the Book. So the Fatiha is the one surah that can't be left out.
Schools of law differ on one detail. Many say every worshipper recites it in each unit. Hanafi scholars teach that behind an imam you stand silent, and the imam's recitation counts for the whole row.
Either way, it's said in every unit. The Qur'an itself seems to point to this. In Surah al-Hijr, God tells the Prophet He has given him seven of the oft-repeated verses, and the great Qur'an.
Many commentators, following a hadith in Bukhari, say those seven are the Fatiha, and its nickname comes from there: as-sab' al-mathani, the seven oft-repeated.
In the count printed in many copies today, the bismillah is the first of the seven; some scholars count differently and still arrive at seven.
Now the question repetition raises: doesn't anything said seventeen times a day go numb? Muslim teachers raise it themselves.

Scholars warn against prayer that's only motion, and teachers tell students to slow down and hear one line freshly each time. The repetition is the container. What's poured into it changes from one prayer to the next.

teach.h: THE SAME WORDS, NEVER SAID THE SAME
teach.b: The most repeated words, said by a tired person at dawn and a grieving one at night, are never quite said the same way twice.

how: Muslims recite al-Fatiha standing in every rak'ah of every prayer, seventeen times a day across the five obligatory prayers; in the Hanafi school a worshipper praying behind an imam listens silently while the imam recites.

o: the shortest surah, at the end of the Qur'an
the verses read only at the dawn prayer

games.q: count it up — tap the pairs.

s: the Fatiha is recited only once in each prayer
it's recited in every unit: seventeen times across the five daily prayers.
in the Hanafi school, someone behind the imam stands silent while he recites
the imam's recitation counts for the row.
the seven verses are counted the same way by every scholar
the common count includes the bismillah; some count differently and still reach seven.

games.q: you've said the same seven verses thousands of times, and today they feel numb. what do Muslim teachers usually say?
o: slow down and hear one line freshly.
say it faster to get through it.
games.why: slow down. scholars warn against prayer that's only motion, and the advice is to hear one line as if for the first time.

practice: Say the seven verses once now, slowly, aloud or silently, the way you'd say them if you'd never said them before. If you don't pray, sit with the opening line, Praise be to Allah, or just with the number seventeen.

wordCard.voice: Seven verses. Al-Fatiha, the seven oft-repeated, recited in every unit of every prayer: seventeen times a day in the obligatory prayers alone. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the seven oft-repeated, a name for al-Fatiha drawn from 15:87.

carryVoice: Your line: the most repeated words. Seventeen times a day, and each one its own. See you tomorrow.
